hello.note: Literally "how are you?", from Spanish ¿cómo está? Add po to be polite: Kumusta po

good-morning.note: Add po for elders and strangers: Magandang umaga po

good-night.note: Both good evening and good night. At bedtime family and friends also say Tulog na (too-LOG nah), time to sleep

goodbye.note: Sounds final. People more often say Sige (SEE-geh), okay then, or Ingat (EE-ngaht), take care

please.note: Literally "I ask a favour". In everyday requests paki- goes on the verb (pakiulit, please repeat), and po makes it polite

thank-you.note: Po makes it polite; to friends just salamat. The reply is walang anuman (wah-LAHNG ah-noo-MAHN)

yes.note: The polite yes, for elders and strangers. Oo (oh-OH) is the plain yes

no.note: Hindi is no and po makes it polite. It ends in a catch in the throat

excuse-me.note: Sorry. To get past someone or get attention, Filipinos often just say excuse me po

my-name.note: Ako is I, and si goes before a person's name. Ikaw is you; kayo (kah-YOH) is politer

speak-english.note: Ba makes it a question. Most people in the Philippines speak some English

hundred.note: Isang is isa (one) joined to the next word with -ng

thousand.note: Prices are in pesos, and people often give them in English or in Spanish numbers: one fifty, or singkwenta (50)

hundred-thousand.note: Written ₱100,000, with commas as in English

how-much.note: Point and say Magkano po ito? (mahg-KAH-noh poh ee-TOH), how much is this?

would-like.note: May I have..., for asking for something. Ng is said nang. The audio uses tubig (water) as the example

i-want.note: Gusto means want or like. The audio uses ito (this one) as the example

do-you-have.note: Put the item after may. May tubig po ba? = Do you have water?

too-expensive.note: Naman softens it, like "that's a bit pricey"

discount.note: Tawad is a discount. Normal in markets, not in malls

card.text: Tumatanggap po ba kayo ng credit card?
card.say: too-mah-TAHNG-gahp poh bah kah-YOH nahng KREH-dit kahrd
card.note: Phone payments with GCash are common too

bill.note: The English word is what everyone uses. Or catch the waiter's eye and draw a box in the air

checkout-time.note: Anong oras? means what time? for anything

wifi.text: Ano po ang password ng Wi-Fi?
wifi.say: ah-NOH poh ahng PAHS-werd nahng WYE-fye
wifi.note: Mixing in English words like this is normal, and called Taglish

toilet.note: CR, for comfort room, is what everyone calls the toilet. Nasaan po ang ...? means where is ...?

taxi.text: Pwede po bang tumawag ng taxi?
taxi.say: PWEH-deh poh bahng too-mah-WAHG nahng TAHK-see
taxi.note: Grab is the usual ride app

train.note: In Manila the city lines are the LRT and the MRT

bus.note: Jeepneys, the long shared jeeps, are the cheapest way around

where-train-station.text: Nasaan po ang istasyon ng tren?
where-train-station.say: nah-sah-AHN poh ahng is-tahs-YON nahng tren

where-bus-station.text: Nasaan po ang terminal ng bus?
where-bus-station.say: nah-sah-AHN poh ahng ter-mee-NAHL nahng boos

which-train.text: Aling tren po ang papunta sa ...?
which-train.say: ah-LING tren poh ahng pah-POON-tah sah
which-train.note: Papunta sa means going to. The audio uses Makati as the example
which-train.spoken: Aling tren po ang papunta sa Makati?

two-tickets.text: Pwede po bang bumili ng dalawang tiket papunta sa ...?
two-tickets.say: PWEH-deh poh bahng boo-mee-LEE nahng dah-lah-WAHNG TEE-ket pah-POON-tah sah
two-tickets.note: Dalawang is two; tatlong (3) or apat na (4) for more. The audio uses Baguio as the example city
two-tickets.spoken: Pwede po bang bumili ng dalawang tiket papunta sa Baguio?

trip-length.note: The audio uses Baguio as the example city
trip-length.spoken: Gaano po katagal papunta sa Baguio?

delicious.note: Sarap means tasty; ang turns it into an exclamation

allergic.note: Filipinos use the English word. Add the food: ... sa mani = to peanuts

love-dish.note: Doubling gusto, like, makes it love

table-for-two.note: Dalawa is two; tatlo (3) or apat (4) for more

menu.text: Pwede po bang makita ang menu?
menu.say: PWEH-deh poh bahng mah-KEE-tah ahng MEH-noo

beer.note: San Miguel is the classic local beer

coffee.note: Often instant, with sugar and creamer already in. Barako is strong local coffee

water.note: Ask for mineral water if you want bottled

cheers.note: Mabuhay! (mah-BOO-hye), long live, is the formal toast

help.note: Saklolo! (sahk-LOH-loh) is a more desperate cry for help

pharmacy.note: Botika comes from Spanish botica. Signs also say pharmacy or drugstore
